title: Encapsulation and Validation
learningObjectives: Validate values before modifying private state.
Provide controlled access to object data.
Distinguish read-only getters from mutating methods.
Test valid, boundary and rejected updates.

understand.concept: Encapsulation combines private state with public operations that validate changes. Invariants are rules that must remain true for an object.
understand.whyItMatters: Validation prevents invalid states from spreading through a program.
understand.explain: Validate inputs in public methods and keep invariant rules consistent.

examples.title: Validate setter
examples.code: class Age{public:bool set(int n){if(n<0||n>120)return false;value=n;return true;}int get()const{return value;}private:int value=0;};
examples.explanation: Invalid values are rejected before state changes.

examples.title: Invariant method
examples.code: class BankAccount{public:bool deposit(double n){if(n<=0)return false;balance+=n;return true;}double get()const{return balance;}private:double balance=0;};
examples.explanation: The method preserves the rule that deposits must be positive.

examples.title: Private state prevents bypass
examples.code: class Score{public:void set(int n){if(n>=0&&n<=100)score=n;}int get()const{return score;}private:int score=0;};
examples.explanation: External code cannot assign invalid score directly.

examples.title: Safe read access
examples.explanation: Read-only getter exposes a value without exposing mutable state.

examples.title: Validate construction
examples.explanation: Constructor validates a relationship between values; include stdexcept.

practise.guidedTask: For Encapsulation and Validation, trace every example. List each type, object, member, initial value, access path, and state change. Identify where encapsulation or initialization affects correctness.
practise.independentTask: Create a small C++ model focused on Encapsulation and Validation (such as a Point, Student, Product, or Account). Include multiple objects, initialization, at least one operation/member access, and test normal, boundary and invalid states. Explain which fields should be public or private and why.
hints: Define the type and its responsibilities before creating objects.
Initialize members deliberately and trace their values.
Use dot for objects and arrow only for pointers.
Keep fields private when they must enforce rules.
Test object creation, valid operations and rejected updates.
